Garland TX Police Incidents

The City of Garland publishes a weekly PDF of selected police incidents. This site turns that PDF into a map you can actually read — and a list you can skim.

Reading the map

Every incident is drawn as a box covering a block, not a pin on a building. Hover a box for the offence, click it for the full record.

The panel in the bottom-right corner lists every incident in the report. Clicking a row jumps the map to it. Incidents that have no box are greyed out but still listed, so the report reads the same whether or not a location could be resolved.

Where the numbers come from

Everything here is derived from the City of Garland's Crime Statistics & Maps page — specifically the "Previous Week Selected Incident Report" PDF. No data is added, and nothing is filtered out.

Because the city publishes the previous week, the map always trails real time by a week or more. It also covers selected offence categories only — murder, sexual assault, aggravated assault, robbery, burglary, theft, motor vehicle theft and criminal mischief — so it is not a complete picture of police activity.

The incident browser is built from a second source: the same page's monthly Crime Watch reports, 53 of them going back to February 2022. Those are kept in their own tables and never mixed with the weekly figures — the two overlap in time, and at different grains there is no honest way to tell one duplicate from two real incidents that share a block, a day and an offence.

Twelve of those months are slightly short. Each report ends every district block with the total it claims for that district, and for those twelve the totals add up to 23 more incidents than the documents actually contain — the rows are not in the PDF text at all, in either extraction mode. A month with a shortfall says so on its own brief. The other 41 months reconcile exactly.

How locations are estimated

The PDF never gives a house number. It reports a block, like 37XX W BUCKINGHAM RD. So a box is the honest shape for this data: the incident happened somewhere along that block.

Each block is looked up against OpenStreetMap, and only results that match a real street address are used. Where both ends of a block resolve, the box spans them; where only one does, it's a fixed box roughly 150 metres across. A typical box is about 120 m on its longest side.

Boxes are approximations, and a few of them will be wrong. Treat them as "this block, give or take" rather than an address. If a lookup can't be pinned to a real address at all, the incident is left off the map instead of being drawn somewhere plausible-looking but false.

What isn't on the map

  • Confidential addresses. The city withholds the location for some incidents — typically sexual assaults and offences involving children. These are listed with their date and district only.
  • Locations that can't be resolved. Freeway blocks (LBJ FRWY), major roads with no address data, streets too new to be in OpenStreetMap, and rows where the city left the address column blank.

How it's built

  1. Download the weekly PDF from the city's document centre.
  2. Extract every incident from the PDF text — date, offence, location and district — and record which week the report covers.
  3. Relabel the offence codes with a language model, turning THEFT-MOTOR VEHICLE-$2,500 L/T $30,000 into Motor Vehicle Theft.
  4. Store the week in a local database, skipping incidents already recorded so a re-run can't double-count.
  5. Geocode each block against OpenStreetMap and build the boxes.
  6. Render the map and the incident list.

Roadmap

  • DoneKeep every week in one database. Past reports are retained and tagged by week, ready for comparison.
  • Show history in the UI. The weeks are stored but the map still only renders the latest one — no trends or week-over-week view yet.
  • Filter by district and offence category.
  • Highlight violent and aggravated offences.
  • Refresh automatically. Publishing a new week is still run by hand.
